This page sets up the Claude desktop app's Code tab for work on rtfreporter,
tflspec or tflplanner. Read [Developing with AI agents](ai-agents.html) first:
it says what the set-up is for. Come back to that page for the workflow when
you are done.

The facts here come from Anthropic's Claude Code documentation, read on
2026-11-08 (see the links). The app's own screens change often. Where the
documentation does not show a screen, the step is marked **(to check)**.

## Open the repository

1. Clone the repository with `git`. A contributor clones a fork. A maintainer
   (a Collaborator) clones `ichirio/rtfreporter` (*Contributor vs Collaborator*
   in `CONTRIBUTING.md`).
2. In the Code tab, use the project folder control, next to the environment
   selector, and choose the clone's folder.
3. To keep the work apart from your main checkout, turn on **Worktree** before
   you start the session. It is off by default. Then Claude works in its own Git
   worktree, under `<project-root>/.claude/worktrees/` by default. Those
   folders show up as untracked files in `git status`. Pull request #935 adds
   `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore`; until you have it, stage named files,
   never `git add .`.
   You can run several sessions in parallel, one per piece of work; each has its
   own project folder, and its own worktree when **Worktree** is on.
4. Make the topic branch: ask Claude to run `git checkout -b <type>/<issue>-<slug>`
   from the right base. A contributor branches from `main` and opens the pull
   request against `main`; a maintainer's branch goes to `next`
   (*Branching & collaboration* in `CONTRIBUTING.md`).
   **(To check:** whether the app has its own branch picker.**)**

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop>

## The environment

The agent's commands must see the work library and the work home, not yours
([section 2 of the shared article](ai-agents.html#the-environment)).

* In the app, put `KEY=value` lines in a **saved local environment** and start
  the session from it. Put `R_LIBS_USER`, `HOME`, `R_USER_CACHE_DIR`,
  `R_USER_DATA_DIR`, `R_USER_CONFIG_DIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP`, `TMPDIR` and
  `WORK_ROOT` there. If you use the hooks below, put `TFL_HOOK_RSCRIPT` (and,
  for a maintainer making a release, `TFL_ALLOW_RELEASE_EDIT`) there too.
  **(To check:** whether Windows paths with a drive letter
  need quoting in that editor.**)**
* The `env` block of `~/.claude/settings.json` is a poor place for these. The
  desktop page says Claude Code ignores a `settings.json` value when the
  variable is already in the environment that the app starts the session with,
  or when the app sets the variable itself. Which of your variables that
  catches depends on your machine. Using the saved local environment is this
  article's advice.
* Tell the agent which R to call, by its full path, in the instruction file
  (next section).

Then ask Claude to run the check script from the shared article. Claude has not
read the article, so paste the script into the chat first, and then write:

> Save the script above as `check-env.R` outside the repository, run it with
> the project's R, and show me the output.

It must end with `Environment OK.` If it stops, fix the environment before
anything else.

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop>

## Instructions

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` at the start of each session. It reads `AGENTS.md`
only when there is no `CLAUDE.md` in the folder or above it (this needs Claude
Code 2.1.277 or later). This repository already has a `CLAUDE.md`. It starts with
`@AGENTS.md`, which imports the shared file, and then adds the notes for
Claude Code. Keep it that way: do not create a second one.

That `CLAUDE.md` already holds most of what an agent needs: the R path, the
rule on `Version` and `NEWS.md`, and the tests and lint before a pull request.
Add only what is missing. For example, these two lines:

```markdown
- After the `pre-pr` skill below is added, run it (`/pre-pr`) before you open a pull request.
- Stop and ask before you push, install into any library other than the work library, or delete files.
```

`CLAUDE.md` is a tracked file, so a line you add lands in your pull request.
Commit it only if it helps every contributor, and say so in the pull request.
A line only for you goes in `CLAUDE.local.md` at the project root, which you
add to `.gitignore` (the memory page describes this).

To confirm that the file was read, ask: "Which instructions did you load for
this repository?" The answer should name `CLAUDE.md`, and the text it imports
from `AGENTS.md`. The Claude Code documentation describes a `/memory` command
that lists the memory files, and `/context all`, which lists those loaded at
launch. **(To check:** whether the desktop app offers them, and where.**)**

An instruction file is context, not a lock. For a rule that must hold, use a
hook (below).

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory>

## Permissions

Claude asks before it edits files or runs most commands. The app has permission
modes: Manual, Accept edits, Plan, Auto and Bypass
permissions. For this work use **Manual** or **Accept edits**. Do not use
Bypass permissions outside a sandbox, such as a container; the documentation
says the same.

Allow the commands you run often, and set the ones you want to decide
yourself to **ask**: Claude then stops and asks you each time. (A `deny` rule
would block the command outright.) The rules go in `.claude/settings.json` (shared) or
`.claude/settings.local.json` (yours). The R path below is an example:

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git status *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(git log *)",
      "Bash(\"C:/Program Files/R/R-4.6.1/bin/Rscript.exe\" *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(rm *)"
    ]
  }
}
```

Two cautions. The first is in the permissions page: a rule matches the command
as written, so `git -C . push` is not matched by `Bash(git push *)`. The page
says a `deny` or `ask` rule is not a security boundary. Treat these rules as a
guide and use a hook for a rule that must hold. The second is this
article's own advice, not the documentation's: an allowed `Rscript` can run any
R code, so allow it only after the environment check passes. **(To check:** how
the permissions page's rules treat a quoted path with spaces, as in the example
above.**)**

The `ask` list above keeps `git push` and `rm` with you: a push goes through
you, as a person. Installing into any library other than the work library is
not a rule here; the instruction lines above cover it. The permissions page
lists `allow`, `ask` and `deny`, and checks them in the order deny, ask, allow.

Sources: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions>,
<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop>

## The pre-PR check

A **skill** is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. A project skill lives in
`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; commit it to share it. Local sessions in the
desktop app load personal skills from `~/.claude/skills/` and project skills
from the repository. You start it with `/<name>`. This example is
`.claude/skills/pre-pr/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: pre-pr
description: The checks to run before opening a pull request in rtfreporter, tflspec or tflplanner.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Run these in order. Stop at the first failure and report it.

1. Run the tests of the changed area.
2. Run `lintr::lint_package()`. It must report 0 lints.
3. List the `pkg::` uses and `requireNamespace()` calls added in the diff, and
   check each is declared in `DESCRIPTION`.
4. When a change in tflspec can break tflplanner, run tflplanner's tests too.
5. Report each result in the pull request description, in the form the pull request template asks for.

Do not edit `NEWS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` or `Version:`.
```

`disable-model-invocation: true` means only you start it. Then type `/pre-pr`
in the prompt box. The desktop page says the slash menu includes project skills
from your codebase, so `/pre-pr` is listed there.

This is a faster subset for each change, not the four pre-push checks of
`CONTRIBUTING.md` (`R CMD check --as-cran`, `devtools::test()`,
`pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` and lintr). CI runs the full set, and so does a
maintainer before a release.

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills>

## Checks on each edit

A **hook** is a command that Claude Code runs at a fixed point. Hooks are set
in `.claude/settings.json`. A `PreToolUse` hook runs before a tool call and
can block it with exit code 2; the message on stderr is what Claude sees. A
`PostToolUse` hook runs after it: it cannot undo the edit, only report back.
The matcher `Edit|Write` selects file edits, and the file's path is in
`tool_input.file_path`.

An example set of two hooks is in `.claude/`, on the branch of pull request
#935. Once #935 is merged into `next`, and `next` into `main`, the repository
holds it. (`.claude` is left out of the package build, so it is in the
repository, not in the installed package.) The hook commands call `bash`; on
Windows that means Git Bash, with `bash` on the path. The two hooks:

* `hooks/guard-version-news.sh` (`PreToolUse`) refuses an edit to `NEWS.md` or
  `CHANGELOG.md`, and an edit to `DESCRIPTION` that touches its `Version:` line, with a message
  that says why: a pull request leaves them to the release. A maintainer making
  a release sets `TFL_ALLOW_RELEASE_EDIT=1`. A whole-file `Write` of
  `DESCRIPTION` is refused too, because its text always holds `Version:`. Change
  other fields with `Edit`.
* `hooks/lint-changed.sh` (`PostToolUse`) lints a changed file under `R/` and
  sends the lints back to Claude. The repository lints `R/` only, as `.lintr`
  and `CONTRIBUTING.md` do. The hook runs only when `TFL_HOOK_RSCRIPT` names the
  `Rscript` of your work set-up. The library it reads is the one the session's
  environment sets (`R_LIBS_USER`), so set the work library there too. Unset,
  it does nothing.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "bash \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/guard-version-news.sh\"", "timeout": 10 }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "bash \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/lint-changed.sh\"", "timeout": 120 }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**What has been tested.** The facts in this paragraph, and the one about
`$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` below, were seen in a test in the desktop app's Code tab
on Windows, not taken from the documentation. In a session opened on the
repository: an edit to `NEWS.md` and an edit to the
`Version:` line were refused with the hook's message; an edit to another
`DESCRIPTION` field, and writing and deleting an R file, went through. The app
asked nothing before running the project's hooks, and has no `/hooks` screen.
The lint hook has been tested by giving its script the input a tool call sends;
in the app it was not run, since `TFL_HOOK_RSCRIPT` was not set. **(To check:**
the lint hook in the app, with `TFL_HOOK_RSCRIPT` set.**)**

**`$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`** is set for hook commands, and the hooks use it to
find their scripts. It is not set in the agent's own Bash shell: a command the
agent runs sees it empty.

If hooks do not run in your set-up, the pre-PR check and CI cover the same
rules.

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks>

## Then

Back to [the workflow in the shared article](ai-agents.html#the-workflow):
issue, small branch, test first, pre-PR check, pull request. After you open the
pull request, the app shows it in the **Changes** card with the status of its CI
checks; the documentation says this needs the GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and
signed in.

Source: <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop>
